title: The Computer That Almost Ran a Country
subject: Project Cybersyn, Chile, 1971–1973

chapters.title: The Room That Shouldn’t Exist
chapters.summary: Cold open (this slice, about 90 seconds) and the opening of the story.

narration.text: In 1972, a group of engineers in Chile were building something that looked like it belonged on the bridge of a science-fiction spaceship.
And the whole thing was designed to help run a country’s economy.
Now, before you picture some enormous supercomputer quietly making decisions about an entire nation, there’s something you should know.
Most of the information feeding this system arrived through machines that were essentially glorified electric typewriters.
And the displays? They were considerably less sophisticated than they looked.
The people building it weren’t just trying to invent a better computer. They were trying to invent a different way to organize an economy.

One where factories could respond to problems faster. Where government decisions could be informed by current production data. And where the people doing the work might actually have some influence over how the system operated.
Some of it worked. Much of it was never finished.
And less than two years after the project began, the entire future it represented was gone.
And it’s one of the strangest technological experiments of the twentieth century.

claims.text: During 1972 a group of engineers in Chile was building the operations room.
claims.note: Check construction dates of the room (1972–73) against Medina ch. 4–5.

claims.text: The operations room had seven chairs.
claims.note: Check count and arrangement against Medina and photographs.

claims.text: The chairs had buttons built into the armrests.
claims.note: Check what the buttons were wired to. The narration does not claim they controlled the live system.

claims.text: The system was designed to help run the Chilean economy.
claims.note: Intent, not demonstrated capability: "help coordinate state-managed industry" is closer to the sources than "run".

claims.text: A telex network linked enterprises to the centre in Santiago.
claims.note: Check the extent of the network and which enterprises were connected. The map in the video is schematic.

claims.text: Most of the information fed to the system arrived by telex machines.
claims.note: "Glorified electric typewriters" is a narrator’s characterisation. Confirm the "most" and the machines used.

claims.text: The room’s displays were much less sophisticated than they appeared (not computer-driven graphics).
claims.note: Confirm how the screens produced their images before this line is final.

claims.text: Stafford Beer, Fernando Flores, Gui Bonsiepe and Salvador Allende were central people in the story.
claims.note: Check each role description on the name cards.

claims.text: One aim was for factories to respond to problems faster.
One aim was for government decisions to be informed by current production data.
One aim was for workers to have some influence over how the system operated.
claims.note: Worker participation was an ideal of the design; scholarship disagrees about how far it was realised. The narration says "might", which is right. Keep it as intent.

claims.text: Some parts of the system worked, including use during the October 1972 truck owners’ strike.
claims.note: How much the system mattered in the strike is contested. The line "Some of it worked" is safe; any stronger claim needs a source.

claims.text: Much of the project was never finished.
The project ended less than two years after it began (Sept 1973 coup).
claims.note: Depends on the start date: first contact with Beer was in 1971. Check the month so "less than two years" holds.

claims.text: "One of the strangest technological experiments of the twentieth century."
claims.note: Editorial judgement, presented as the narrator’s view.

editorialNotes.text: Narration is the owner’s draft, split at sentence level only. Nothing was reworded. Historical wording marked in the dossier still needs checking against the sources.
